source.title: Capability Emergence Can Be Forecast: Per-Seed, In Advance, With Calibrated Intervals, Certified False Alarms, and a Blind Pre-Registered Gate

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests emergence of an induction-related capability in pretrained language-model checkpoints, a setting beyond the original small algorithmic grokking tasks.
record.gate_note: The grokking section reports forecasting performance on existing grokking runs, but does not report training-versus-test accuracy or a training-set-size comparison. The synthetic language-model fleet is not realistic pretraining data. Rows below cover the public pretrained-checkpoint results relevant to V4.
record.test_reason: No result here bears on whether any version holds. The grokking half (466 runs) uses existing grokking runs as a substrate and reports only forecaster performance: lead time, false alarms and calibration transfer. It reports no train-vs-test accuracy, training-set-size dependence or circuit measures. The language-model half measures the induction-head phase change in pretraining. That change happens early (about 2.1B tokens in Pythia) and abruptly, but the study shows no generalization delayed after fitting the training data. It is abrupt capability emergence, a related but different construct from grokking-like delayed generalization (V4). The reader's V4 links and 'supports' labels are therefore unwarranted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that, for a named capability with a known mechanistic precursor in small transformers, emergence timing is forecastable per run in advance. Their forecasts have calibrated intervals and certified false alarms, and they follow a multiplicative law (t_event ≈ 1.19 × t_anchor). Public checkpoints confirm that the precursor leads the capability, but those checkpoints cannot test per-seed forecasting. The grokking half contributes evaluation methodology and failed probes, not claims about grokking itself. Frontier applicability is not established.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a forecasting protocol using precursor alarms, behavioral events, manufactured negatives, and checkpoint analysis; it does not reproduce the original grokking training-and-test accuracy experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports precursor alarms earlier than loss thresholds on 4/5 Pythia suites, with lead varying from 1–8 stages; public checkpoint granularity limits event-time resolution.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia, OLMo-1 and OLMo-2 checkpoints, the previous-token head forms a stage or more before the induction/copy capability cliffs. All five Pythia suites cliff at about 2.1B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A mechanistic precursor circuit forms before abrupt capability emergence in LM pretraining, and per-run timing can be forecast from it.

fits_no_version.finding: The pythia-70m induction score falls from 0.93 to 0.36 at 67B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capabilities that emerged during pretraining can partially regress later in training.

fits_no_version.finding: In an algorithmic grokking corpus, structure-complete but blocked negatives carry more 'progress' signal than true positives show before their events. No forecaster passed at a 5% false-alarm rate (kill K1/K8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal progress-like signals may not discriminate runs that will grok from look-alike runs that will not.

record.problems: The realistic-pretraining evidence is limited to public checkpoint trajectories, whose granularity bounds event timing. The study states that all five Pythia suites cliff at the same token count, so they cannot establish per-seed forecasting there. Evidence concerns one capability and small language models; frontier applicability is not established.
record.rows_left_out: No additional public-checkpoint results bearing on V4 were omitted. Grokking forecaster performance and the synthetic language-model fleet are not rows for the listed versions because they do not measure the specified accuracy, mechanism, regime-switch, efficiency, algorithm-identity, or optimizer-artifact claims.

untested.parts: All of it: train/test accuracy gap, chance-to-perfect jump, and dependence on training-set size.
Gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures tied to the circuit. The grokking forecasters are reported only as method performance.
Switching via initialization scale or weight norm. The MNIST Omnigrok runs are used only as a forecasting substrate.
Delayed generalization after fitting in LLM pretraining or fine-tuning. Only early induction emergence is measured.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' labels and the T3 tranche rest on equating induction-head emergence with grokking. The paper makes no such claim about delayed generalization, so none of the extracted rows bears on any version. The cited original source (arXiv:2301.05217) appears only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test training accuracy saturation, test accuracy rising from chance after overfitting, or whether smaller training sets require more optimization.

It reports a previous-token precursor preceding induction emergence, but does not test gradual formation of a grokking generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or whether progress measures anticipate a grokking jump.
The study does not test whether grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data can be switched by initialization scale or weight norm.
The checkpoint evidence concerns induction-related behavior in public pretrained models; it does not test fine-tuning, frontier-scale models, or other realistic-data capabilities.
No critical dataset size, low-norm efficiency account, or ungrokking threshold is tested.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
It does not test whether adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point limits in the softmax cause the delay.

rows.subject: Pythia public suites (5 suites; 70m/160m/410m, standard and deduped)
rows.operation_detail: Measured behavioral copy advantage at a public checkpoint.
rows.note: The paper says the capability cliff occurs one stage later; the public checkpoints do not resolve within-run timing.
rows.check: This is the pre-cliff value of copy advantage (0.022 at 1.07B tokens), not a partial effect. Induction emergence with no train/test gap does not measure V4's delayed generalization.

rows.subject: Pythia public suites (5 suites; 70m/160m/410m, standard and deduped)
rows.operation_detail: Measured induction score at a public checkpoint.
rows.note: The score is reported at the checkpoint preceding the stated cliff.
rows.check: This is the pre-cliff induction score (0.019), a baseline-like value rather than a partial effect. It is not a measure of delayed generalization.

rows.subject: Pythia public suites (5 suites; 70m/160m/410m, standard and deduped)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the previous-token-head precursor at a public checkpoint.
rows.baseline: about 10× baseline; exact baseline not stated
rows.note: At this checkpoint the precursor is reported as already present while induction remains low.
rows.check: The previous-token precursor score (0.37) concerns precursor-before-induction ordering, not grokking-like delay.

rows.subject: Pythia public suites (5 suites; 70m/160m/410m, standard and deduped)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the later behavioral and induction capability cliff.

conditions.value: one stage after 1.07B tokens; all five suites cliff at approximately 2.1B tokens

rows.baseline: At 1.07B tokens: copy advantage 0.022 and induction score 0.019
rows.note: The paper describes both measures as cliffing after the precursor is already elevated.
rows.check: The induction/copy cliff at about 2.1B tokens is abrupt emergence early in pretraining, not generalization delayed after memorization. Its baseline should be the 1.07B-token checkpoint values, which the row gives correctly.

rows.subject: Pythia public suites (5 suites; 70m/160m/410m, standard and deduped)
rows.operation_detail: Compared precursor alarm timing with capability and best-case loss-threshold timing.
rows.measure: precursor lead over capability and loss threshold
rows.baseline: Best-case loss threshold granted an oracle sweep
rows.value: Precursor alarmed earlier on 4/5 suites and never post-event; leads of 1–8 stages
rows.note: The paper also says the pre-registered prediction failed in both directions: the precursor led by more than predicted and loss was stronger than predicted.
rows.check: This compares the study's own forecasting alarm with a loss-threshold baseline. It is method performance and should not be a claim row.

rows.subject: OLMo-1

rows.note: At this checkpoint the capability score is below its stated threshold.
rows.check: The OLMo-1 precursor score bears on precursor ordering, not grokking.

rows.subject: OLMo-1
rows.operation_detail: Measured induction-related capability score at the intermediate checkpoint.
rows.note: The precursor is reported formed while the capability remains below threshold; the later ordinal lead is 8→12B tokens.
rows.check: 0.71 nats is the pre-threshold capability at 8B tokens, not a partial effect. It is not a grokking measure.

rows.check: The OLMo-2 precursor score bears on precursor ordering, not grokking.

rows.check: -0.14 nats is the capability being absent before emergence, not a partial effect. It is not a grokking measure.

rows.subject: pythia-70m

rows.check: This is late induction regression in pythia-70m, which no version covers. 'Reversed' is not meaningful against any version.
